ENTIRELY — and docs/MCP.md tells developers to put their own MCP servers there, so

THIS FILE STILL WINS per key; mcp.servers merges by SERVER NAME so a team pin and a

_setup: READ THIS BEFORE FIRST USE.
The values below are a STARTING POINT measured on one fleet (Apple M3 Max / 64 GB /
Ollama 0.32.3, 2026-07-31). They are a worked example of the schema, not a
recommendation for your hardware.
Before first use:
1. tools/localcoder --doctor      — see what this machine actually has
2. update approved_models, digests and min_ram_gb from YOUR results
OPTIONAL: tools/localcoder_bench.py measures the models you are considering. Nothing
fails without it — not setup.sh, not --doctor, not CI. Run it when onboarding a
machine, adding a model to approved_models, changing num_ctx, or upgrading Ollama.
Skip it otherwise. Runbook: docs/benchmarks/README.md
DIGESTS: an empty digest means 'not pinned yet' and is SKIPPED, not failed. Leave it
empty rather than inheriting someone else's — a pin you did not set will fail every
fresh clone the moment that upstream tag is re-published, with no obvious cause. Pin it
once you have pulled the model you intend to keep (--doctor prints the value to use).
Delete this file entirely to opt out: this project then uses the DEVICE config at
~/.config/localcoder/config.json if one exists, else env vars and built-in defaults.
(.localcoderrc was the pre-fleet per-project file and was removed in v0.5.0.)
CHOOSING num_ctx — THE COST DEPENDS ON THE RUNNER, NOT ON THE MODEL.
Measured 2026-08-09, Apple M5 Max / 64 GB / ollama 0.32.5, one server, ~20-token prompt:
num_ctx     gemma4:26b-mxfp8 (MLX)    qwen3-coder:30b-a3b-q8_0 (GGUF)
131,072         26.94 GB  (unchanged)       45.46 GB  (+10 GB, unused)
MLX SIZES THE CACHE TO THE SEQUENCE. A window you do not fill is free — the two
numbers above are identical, not close. What it costs is ~70 KB per token actually
sent (26.94 GB idle -> 33.1 GB holding 88,998 tokens), so a FULL 131,072 window is
about +9 GB, and only while you are using it.
GGUF PRE-ALLOCATES THE WHOLE WINDOW at load. The +10 GB above was paid for a
fifteen-token prompt. Set `num_ctx` per model in approved_models for these.
THE OLD TABLE HERE MEASURED ONE GGUF MODEL AND WAS READ AS A LAW ABOUT ALL OF THEM.
It said 'RAM moves +1 GB then +4 GB' and concluded memory cost accelerates while
speed cost flattens. That is true, of qwen3-coder:30b-a3b-q8_0. Six of the eight
models below are MLX, including the default, and for those the memory axis of that
conclusion is simply absent. The generation-speed half held for both runners.
THE HALVING, WHICH IS THE PART THAT ACTUALLY BITES.
The llama.cpp runner reads num_ctx/2 and reserves the rest for generation. Past that
it keeps the first FOUR tokens and drops the front of the prompt — your standards and
gotchas — and tells the client NOTHING. From this machine's own ollama log:
msg="truncating input prompt" limit=16386 prompt=32832 keep=4   (num_ctx  32,768)
msg="truncating input prompt"  limit=4098 prompt=18997 keep=4   (num_ctx   8,192)
Measured against the same 200,000-character prompt at num_ctx 8,192: the GGUF model
received 4,098 tokens and answered in 2.3s; the MLX model received all 63,431 and
took 58.6s. The truncated call was the FAST one. That is the whole problem — a
prompt losing 94% of itself presents as the tool getting quicker, and the reply
still reads plausibly, because the model answers the question it was left with.
MLX did not truncate at any window tested.
So the working ceiling is num_ctx/2 on GGUF and num_ctx on MLX. `localcoder --where`
prints it as `max prompt`. localcoder warns before the call from an estimate and
reports `truncated` after it from the token count the server returns — the second
one is the reliable half, because it is evidence rather than arithmetic.
WHY THIS PROJECT PINS 131,072.
Every model in approved_models supports at least 131,072 natively (six support
262,144; the two hermes3 tags cap at 131,072), so it is the largest window every
approved model can honour rather than a round number. It is free on the default,
and it lifts the GGUF working ceiling from 16,386 tokens to 65,538 — which matters
now that tools/api_digest.py makes repo-scale context a normal thing to send: this
repo's own tools/ + ai/ digest is ~43,000 tokens, i.e. comfortably over the ceiling
the previous 32,768 pin allowed.
IT WAS 32,768 UNTIL 2026-08-09, and the reasoning was sound when written: drafting
prompts ran ~1.7k tokens, so 32,768 was ~3x the largest prompt ever observed. The
digest changed what gets sent; the pin did not follow.
THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IS USUALLY EVICTION, NOT SPEED. A 45 GB resident model on a
64 GB machine leaves little room for the editor and asset tooling the same developer
is running. Use `localcoder --unload` when you are done drafting.
Changing num_ctx? Re-run tools/install_ollama_service.sh so the server default
follows, and re-measure min_ram_gb for any GGUF model — the floor is tied to the
context it was measured at. MLX floors are NOT scaled to the window, because the
measurement above says the window is free; localcoder skips the scaling for them.
_comment: TEMPLATE — REPLACE THE VALUES BELOW WITH YOUR OWN BEFORE RELYING ON THIS.
The models, digests and RAM floors here are REFERENCE VALUES measured on one
fleet (Apple M3 Max / 64 GB / Ollama 0.32.3, 2026-07-31). They are shipped as a
worked example of the schema, not as a recommendation for your hardware. Until
you edit them, `localcoder --doctor` will correctly report that the pinned model
is not present on your machine.
Three ways to adopt this:
1. Pin your own  — replace default_model/approved_models with tags you have
benchmarked. Get a digest with: ollama show <tag> --modelfile | head -1
or read it from: curl -s localhost:11434/api/tags
2. Keep the reference — pull the tags below and use them as-is.
3. Opt out entirely — DELETE this file. This project then falls back to the
DEVICE config at ~/.config/localcoder/config.json if one exists, else to env
vars and built-in defaults. Nothing breaks; you lose the pinning guarantee,
and each developer's own device file starts deciding. (.localcoderrc was the
pre-fleet per-project file; it was removed in v0.5.0 and is not read.)
WHAT THIS FILE BUYS: every developer on the project runs the same model at the
same settings, so drafts are reproducible between machines and a colleague's
result can be investigated rather than guessed at.
MODEL POLICY: a developer may select any model in approved_models, and nothing
else. LOCALCODER_MODEL naming an unapproved tag is REFUSED. That keeps the door
open for better hardware (a 128 GB machine can run a larger approved model) while
preventing anyone from quietly running something the team has not benchmarked.
Adding a model = a reviewed commit to this file, plus a benchmark row from
tools/localcoder_bench.py so the choice is evidenced rather than asserted.
DIGESTS MATTER: an Ollama tag can be re-published, so two developers pulling on
different days can hold different weights under the same tag. --doctor compares
the installed digest against the pin for the model actually selected.
Windows is not yet tested — the RAM check is sysctl-only and degrades to a skip.
SCOPE — THIS FILE IS THE PROJECT SCOPE, AND IT WINS OUTRIGHT.
localcoder resolves exactly one config: $LOCALCODER_CONFIG, else this file, else the
device config at ~/.config/localcoder/config.json, else built-in defaults. While this
file exists, a developer's device config is IGNORED — including for keys this file
does not set, which fall to built-in defaults instead. That is deliberate: a device
file quietly supplying the keys a project left unset means two developers get
different windows from the same task, with no message, which is the divergence this
file exists to prevent.
localcoder --where     which config is in force, and where every setting came from
To inherit a developer's device defaults on purpose, add:  "extends": "device"
The merge is SHALLOW and this file wins per key. approved_models is never deep-merged
— a device must not be able to add a model to a reviewed registry.
NOTES CARRY MEASUREMENTS, NOT ADJECTIVES — with the date and conditions they were
taken under. 'Faster generation' rots silently; '+16% generation, -67% prefill,
measured 2026-08-05 on M3 Max/64 GB/ollama 0.32.3 at num_ctx 131072, k=3' can be
checked and re-measured. This matters more than it sounds: the alternate below
carried '~34% faster generation, ~35% slower prefill' for weeks. Measured properly it
is +16% generation and -67% PREFILL, with the lowest pass@1 of four models tested —
so the note was wrong in magnitude on one axis, wrong by half on the other, and
silent on quality entirely. An unmeasured adjective in a registry is a decision
nobody can audit.
min_ram_gb IS A FLOOR TO WORK ON, NOT A FLOOR TO FIT IN. Record what the machine
needs to run the model AND everything the developer has open beside it — editor,
browser, asset tooling, containers. A floor that only clears the model itself passes
--doctor on a machine nobody can actually work on, and the failure then arrives as
eviction and stalling mid-draft rather than as a clear refusal up front.
_model_selection: MEASURED SCORECARD — Apple M5 Max / 64 GB / Ollama 0.32.5, 2026-08-07, num_ctx 32,768.
The scorecard belongs in the file where the choice is made. Someone editing
default_model should read the evidence here rather than go hunting for
docs/benchmarks/. Fill it after running BOTH tools — the bench for speed, the eval
for quality — and record the date, machine and num_ctx the rows were taken at.
REPLACE THE ROWS BELOW WITH YOUR OWN; they describe one machine, not a recommendation.
model                          pass@1  solid  prefill   gen   load   RAM   draft
ORDER OF PREFERENCE FOR CODING (1 = reach for this first):
1. qwen3.6:27b-coding-mxfp8   Only model with no failure on either suite. 28 task-runs,
84 samples, zero failures, at two temperatures. Its cost is
PREFILL: 191 tok/s is the slowest here, ~87s to read a
16.5k-token subsystem before it writes a token. Reach for it
when the task is narrow and correctness matters most.
2. qwen3.6:35b-a3b-coding     88% / 11-of-14, and 5.8x the prefill (1110 tok/s, ~15s at
16.5k). THE LONG-CONTEXT CHOICE: when ai/CODING.md's 'send
the subsystem, not the sentence' applies, this is the only
model that reads it at a sane speed and still scores well.
3. gemma4:26b-mxfp8           87% / 8-of-10 in 27 GB — the best score per GB measured.
Untested on the 14-task suite, so treat 87% as generous.
4. qwen3.6:27b-mlx            87% / 8-of-10 in 19 GB, the smallest capable model here.
For a machine that must run other things beside it.
5. qwen3-coder:30b-a3b-q8_0   THE CURRENT default_model, and the weakest of the three
measured on 14 tasks: 67% / 8-of-14. It is by far the
fastest (2634 prefill, 2.3s load, 7.9s draft) and that is
the only reason to keep it. Revisit default_model.
6. qwen3-coder-next:q4_K_M    73% / 5-of-10 for 52 GB. Worst reliability of any qwen
measured. Does not earn its footprint. See RAM note below.
NOT FOR CODING — RETAINED DELIBERATELY:
hermes3:70b-llama3.1-q4_K_M and hermes3:8b-llama3.1-q8_0 scored 53% and 37%, the two
worst results measured, and three of the 8b's failures were runtime crashes (NameError,
IndexError, ZeroDivisionError) — code that does not execute at all. DO NOT SELECT EITHER
FOR DRAFTING.
They stay in the registry for NON-CODING work — security research and agentic tasks,
where a less heavily guardrailed general-purpose model is the point rather than a
defect. THAT USE CASE IS UNMEASURED: every number in this file is execution-graded
Python drafting, which says nothing about instruction-following, refusal behaviour or
tool-calling. Treat their presence as 'kept for evaluation in another role', not as an
endorsement, and measure that role before relying on it.
RAM: EVERY MODEL HERE RAN ON 64 GB at num_ctx 32,768 — none failed to load. But peak
resident leaves very little behind the two largest:
qwen3-coder-next:q4_K_M       52 GB resident -> 12 GB free of 64 (floor: 96 GB)
hermes3:70b-llama3.1-q4_K_M   53 GB resident -> 11 GB free of 64 (floor: 96 GB)
That is not enough to work beside on a 64 GB machine — an editor, a browser and a test
run will not fit in 11 GB. Both are usable only as the sole workload, and both figures
are at 32,768; a larger num_ctx grows the KV cache and neither has been measured there.
TEMPERATURE WAS MEASURED AND CHANGED NOTHING — recorded so nobody repeats it. Pinning
0.3/0.4/0.5 against the tag defaults, six models, moved pass@1 by at most 2 points and
fully-solid counts by ZERO on a 14-task suite. An apparent +10 on a 10-task suite was
that suite hitting its ceiling, not a gain. temperature stays "model". 2026-08-07.
READ 'draft' AND NOT 'prefill/gen' WHEN JUDGING SPEED. The per-token columns are
what the HARDWARE does; the draft column is what a developer WAITS FOR, and they
disagree sharply. Measured downstream 2026-08-05: a model whose prefill was 5.4x
slower than the baseline's produced drafts only 1.6x slower — confirmed on a real
16.5k-token subsystem draft, 130s vs 82s. An earlier version of that scorecard
called the model unusable on the strength of the per-token ratio alone. It was not.
Fixed costs and bounded output lengths dominate a real draft, so a throughput ratio
misreads the wait badly.
THAT LESSON APPLIES TO THE ROWS ABOVE, AND IT WAS RE-LEARNED THE HARD WAY. The
prefill figures here invite dividing 16,500 by tok/s and calling the answer a wait:
that arithmetic gives ~87s for the top model against ~15s for the alternate, and it
was used in this session to argue the alternate was the better choice. It is the
SAME per-token misreading this paragraph documents. No 16.5k-token draft has been
measured on this machine for any model here, so the ~87s is a projection the one
real measurement above suggests will overstate the gap substantially. Measure it
before letting it decide anything.
A SECOND CORRECTION TO THE SAME COLUMN: 'draft' as recorded by localcoder_eval
INCLUDES a cold model load, because the eval stops the model between samples to keep
runs independent. Production sets keepalive 30m and never pays it. Subtract the load
column for a warm figure — doing so reverses the top two rows, 23.2-8.4 = 14.8s
STATE WHY THE DEFAULT IS THE DEFAULT WHEN IT IS NOT THE HIGHEST SCORER, and say what
would change it. Downstream the top-scoring model held 53 GB on a 64 GB fleet floor,
leaving ~11 GB for the editor and asset tooling — it fits and cannot be lived with.
The default was one task behind on an 8-task suite, with more prefill throughput and
9 GB less resident. 'Revisit above 64 GB' is the kind of trigger worth writing down.

qwen3-coder:30b-a3b-q8_0.notes:
APPROVED, NO LONGER THE DEFAULT (2026-08-09). RE-MEASURED 2026-08-09 ON THE 14-TASK SET (fingerprint 8b0bf3cde373), Apple M5 Max / 64 GB / ollama 0.32.5, num_ctx 32768, k=3. The whole field moved when the suite grew from 8 to 14 tasks, and no model's recorded score had been re-taken against it. It scored pass@1 0.69 and 0.67 over two runs, 8/14 fully solid — last of the serious models in the field. Its headline number in this entry used to be '92% (7/8 solid)', measured on an EIGHT-task suite on an M3 Max at num_ctx 131072. The suite grew to 10 and then 14 tasks; the baseline was never re-run against it, and nothing in the published history marked the old figure as taken on a suite that no longer exists — tools/localcoder_history.py grouped rows by (model, digest, num_ctx) and ignored the task-set fingerprint that tools/localcoder_eval.py prints and calls load-bearing. Fixed in the same change.

KEPT APPROVED, AND FOR A SPECIFIC REASON: 2650 tok/s prefill, 4.7x the new default's. That is the model to pass explicitly for repo-scale context — a 38k-token digest prefills in 14s here against 68s on the default. Choose it deliberately, per call, when breadth matters more than the draft being right first time.

Original M3 Max measurement, kept because the runtime comparison in it is still useful: prefill 1082 tok/s, generation 55.5, cold load 2.2s, 39 GB resident, median draft 10.5s at num_ctx 131072. GGUF prefill was UNCHANGED by the 0.32.3->0.32.5 upgrade that moved MLX-MoE +194%, which is worth knowing when choosing a runner. Prefill takes a one-time ~12% step from 32k to 64k and then flattens; generation does not move with num_ctx.

REPO-SCALE PREFILL, CORRECTED 2026-08-09 (same day, later measurement). An earlier version of this entry said this model is 'the model to pass explicitly for repo-scale context — a 38k-token digest prefills in 14s here against 68s on the default'. MEASURED, THE COMPARISON IS THE OTHER WAY ROUND: on a 33,111-token prompt it prefills at 479 tok/s and takes 68.8s, while gemma4:26b-mxfp8 takes 31.9s at 1,113 tok/s. The 68s was real and it was THIS model's, attributed to the other one. The error came from extrapolating a bench-scale rate (2,650 tok/s, measured on ~2k-token prompts) to a prompt sixteen times longer, where it does not hold — see _prefill_note.

SO WHAT IS IT FOR NOW? Short prompts where prefill dominates and quality is adequate: at 2,639 tokens it is still the fastest thing in this registry to first byte. It is not the long-context choice, it is the SMALL-CONTEXT choice, and it costs 45.46 GB at num_ctx 131,072 because GGUF pre-allocates — which is why its window is pinned to 65,536 in this entry rather than following the global.

qwen3.6:35b-a3b-coding-mxfp8.notes:
APPROVED ALTERNATE. MoE ~3B active, coding-tuned, MLX. Measured 2026-08-05 on Apple M3 Max / 64 GB / OLLAMA 0.32.5, num_ctx 131072, bench k=3 and eval k=3: prefill 1050 tok/s (-3% vs the baseline), generation 68.2 (+23%), cold load 12.8s, 36 GB resident, median draft 17.8s. Quality pass@1 83% (6/8 solid), the lowest of four models tested — but on a real 16.5k-token draft it is 2.2x FASTER than the baseline, so it is the long-context choice despite the score. THE RUNTIME VERSION IS PART OF THIS MEASUREMENT: on ollama 0.32.3 the same weights prefilled at 358 tok/s (-67%) and this entry recommended against the model. A PATCH RELEASE MOVED IT +194%. Before that it read '~34% faster generation, ~35% slower prefill' with no date and no conditions, which measurement refuted on both axes. Two corrections to one line is why notes carry figures, dates AND the runtime they were taken on.

REPO-SCALE PREFILL 909 tok/s (2026-08-09), 36.4s for a 33,111-token prompt — second only to the default, and the MoE architecture is why: both models that hold their prefill rate at length here are mixture-of-experts, both dense 27B tags collapse to ~140 tok/s. Worth re-testing as the long-context alternate if the default ever regresses on quality.

qwen3-coder-next:q4_K_M.notes: CANDIDATE — under evaluation on dev/local-model-eval, not approved for use. 80B-A3B MoE; 53 GB resident at num_ctx 131072 on M3 Max, so the floor is 64 to leave room to work beside it. RAM FLOOR RAISED TO 96 GB 2026-08-08, and it is not a fit-in figure: this ran on a 64 GB machine at num_ctx 32,768, peak 52 GB resident. It LOADS in 64 and leaves 12 GB behind it, which is not enough for an editor, a browser and a test run — the case this file's own definition of min_ram_gb names ('a floor that only clears the model itself passes --doctor on a machine nobody can actually work on'). 96 is the floor to WORK on; it is inferred from the measured 52 GB plus working headroom, not measured on a 96 GB machine, and no 96 GB machine was tested. The 52 GB is also at 32,768 only — a larger window grows the KV cache and was not measured.

qwen3.6:27b-coding-mxfp8.notes:
APPROVED — THE QUALITY CEILING, AND THE ONLY MODEL THAT HAS NEVER MISSED. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-09 ON THE 14-TASK SET (fingerprint 8b0bf3cde373), Apple M5 Max / 64 GB / ollama 0.32.5, num_ctx 32768, k=3. The whole field moved when the suite grew from 8 to 14 tasks, and no model's recorded score had been re-taken against it. pass@1 1.00, 14/14 fully solid, over two runs. It is not the default because it costs 23.2-23.9s per draft against 5.5s, and 200s to prefill a 38k-token repo digest at 189 tok/s — a wait that stops people delegating at all, which is the failure this project measured at 0.29% attribution. Pass it explicitly when a draft has to be right first time and the wait is worth it. Dense 27B; 30 GB resident, generation is slow on Apple Silicon by construction.

AND IT IS WORSE THAN IT LOOKS FOR BREADTH, measured 2026-08-09: 131 tok/s on a 33,111-token prompt, i.e. 4 MINUTES 12 SECONDS before it starts writing. This entry already said '200s to prefill a 38k-token repo digest at 189 tok/s'; the real figure at that size is 252s, because 189 was measured on ~2k-token prompts and the rate falls with length. Perfect scores and a four-minute wait are not a trade most tasks should take — pass it a FILE, not a repo.

qwen3.6:27b-mlx.notes:
APPROVED ALTERNATE. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-09 ON THE 14-TASK SET (fingerprint 8b0bf3cde373), Apple M5 Max / 64 GB / ollama 0.32.5, num_ctx 32768, k=3. The whole field moved when the suite grew from 8 to 14 tasks, and no model's recorded score had been re-taken against it. pass@1 93%, 11/14 fully solid, median draft 6.85s, 19 GB resident at num_ctx 65536 — the smallest footprint measured. One run at 14 tasks against the default's two, so treat 93% as provisional. It lost the default slot to gemma4:26b-mxfp8 on all three axes (93 vs 95, 11 vs 13 solid, 6.9s vs 5.5s) after both had scored 87% on the smaller 10-task suite, which is what the earlier comparison used.

REPO-SCALE PREFILL 151 tok/s (2026-08-09): 3 minutes 40 seconds for a 33,111-token prompt, against 31.9s on the default. Smallest footprint measured (22.41 GB loaded at num_ctx 131,072) and the slowest but one to read anything large. A file-sized-context model.

gemma4:26b-mxfp8.notes:
DEFAULT as of 2026-08-09, promoted on measurement. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-09 ON THE 14-TASK SET (fingerprint 8b0bf3cde373), Apple M5 Max / 64 GB / ollama 0.32.5, num_ctx 32768, k=3. The whole field moved when the suite grew from 8 to 14 tasks, and no model's recorded score had been re-taken against it. Two runs, identical: pass@1 95%, 13/14 fully solid, median draft 5.47s and 5.78s. Its single failure was flaky (1/3) on one task, not a hard miss. Prefill 558 tok/s, generation 90.8, 27 GB resident.

WHY IT DISPLACED qwen3-coder:30b-a3b-q8_0: on the same suite, same machine, same day, the previous default scored 0.69 and 0.67 over two runs at 3.4s and 7.9s. This model is +27 points of pass@1 at the same latency. There is no axis on which the swap costs quality; the one thing given up is prefill throughput, 558 against 2650, which matters only for repo-scale context (68s vs 14s on a 38k-token digest).

THIS ENTRY PREVIOUSLY SAID IT WAS NOT PROMOTED, AND THE REASON IS RETIRED HERE RATHER THAN DELETED. It read: 'THE REASON IT IS NOT PROMOTED is qwen3.6:27b-mlx, which scores identically (87%, 8/10) in 19 GB at 5.70s — a model already in this registry dominates it outright on this suite.' That was true of the 10-task suite. On the 14-task suite gemma4 beats 27b-mlx on all three axes: 95 vs 93 pass@1, 13 vs 11 fully solid, 5.5s vs 6.9s. The decision was findable ONLY because whoever wrote it wrote down why — a conclusion with no stated reason cannot be refuted by a later measurement.

CAVEATS KEPT. It is a different model family from the qwen tags this project's drafting brief was written against, so a prompt-following regression would show up as a quality drop this eval may not cover. Prefill 558 is the weak axis and this suite barely tests it at ~2k-token prompts; with tools/api_digest.py making repo-scale context routine, a long-context re-measure could still change the ordering.

AND IT IS ALSO THE REPO-SCALE CHOICE, measured 2026-08-09 rather than inferred. The caveat this entry carried — 'prefill 558 is the weak axis... a long-context re-measure could still change the ordering' — was tested, and it changed the ordering in this model's favour. On a 33k-token prompt it prefills at 1,113 tok/s (31.9s), against 479 for qwen3-coder:30b and 131-151 for the two dense 27B tags. It holds that rate to at least 88,998 tokens (870 tok/s, 102s). The window is free: 26.94 GB resident at num_ctx 32,768 and at 131,072 alike, rising ~70 KB per token actually sent — 33.1 GB while holding 88,998. There is now no axis on which this is not the model to reach for first.

LATENCY FIGURES CORRECTED 2026-08-09 (evening), AND THE CORRECTION IS THE USEFUL PART. The '5.47s and 5.78s' above were taken with a 21 GB model left resident by an unrelated keep-alive — 47 GB of models sharing one 64 GB machine. With the machine to itself the same suite medians 3.96s at num_ctx 32,768 and 4.78s at 131,072.

DO NOT READ THAT 0.8s AS THE COST OF THE WINDOW. Over the same session, generation throughput on this box fell 129.5 -> 70.1 tok/s (-46%) under sustained load, and the 131,072 leg ran second. Five alternating pairs could not separate the window from the drift; the coolest pairs show parity. The honest statement is that the window's effect on generation is BELOW THIS MACHINE'S NOISE FLOOR, which is a weaker claim than 'free' and the only one measured.

QUALITY IS THE PART THAT IS SETTLED: pass@1 95%, 95%, 95%, 98% across four runs spanning both windows and both residency states. The window costs no correctness. Every eval row since 0.5.0 records `co_resident`, so this class of confusion is visible in the data rather than reconstructed from memory.

hermes3:8b-llama3.1-q8_0.notes: REJECTED 2026-08-07 — measured, do not use for coding. Apple M5 Max / 64 GB / OLLAMA 0.32.5, num_ctx 32768, bench 3 runs and eval k=3: prefill 2582 tok/s, generation 60.2, 13 GB resident, median draft 2.84s. Quality pass@1 37% (2/10 solid), the worst in an eight-model field. It is genuinely the cheapest thing here — near-baseline prefill in a THIRD of the memory — and that is the trap: three of its five failing tasks were runtime crashes (NameError, IndexError, ZeroDivisionError), i.e. code that does not execute at all, which a read-through review would have accepted. Kept in the registry as the measured floor, because a field where every model scores 80-100% cannot show whether the suite discriminates.

hermes3:70b-llama3.1-q4_K_M.notes: REJECTED 2026-08-07 — measured, do not use for coding. Apple M5 Max / 64 GB / OLLAMA 0.32.5, num_ctx 32768, bench 3 runs and eval k=3: prefill 255 tok/s, generation 11.0, 53 GB resident, median draft 22.89s. Quality pass@1 53% (3/10 solid). WORST TRADE IN THE FIELD: it costs the most memory of any model measured and generates 8x slower than the baseline, to score 27 points BELOW it. Size is not quality — this 70B scored 47 points under qwen3.6:27b-coding-mxfp8 (53% vs 100%) on the same suite, same day, same machine. Name the comparand: an earlier draft of this line said '34 points under a 27B dense', which is the gap to 27b-mlx (87%), not to the dense 27B it claimed. Two caveats kept deliberately: it is the only q4_K_M model here, and it is general-purpose rather than coding-tuned, so quantisation and training both confound the score. Neither is worth re-testing at 11 tok/s. RAM FLOOR RAISED TO 96 GB 2026-08-08, and it is not a fit-in figure: this ran on a 64 GB machine at num_ctx 32,768, peak 53 GB resident. It LOADS in 64 and leaves 11 GB behind it, which is not enough for an editor, a browser and a test run — the case this file's own definition of min_ram_gb names ('a floor that only clears the model itself passes --doctor on a machine nobody can actually work on'). 96 is the floor to WORK on; it is inferred from the measured 53 GB plus working headroom, not measured on a 96 GB machine, and no 96 GB machine was tested. The 53 GB is also at 32,768 only — a larger window grows the KV cache and was not measured.

approved_models._comment: Optional `prefill_toks`: this model's measured prefill rate on THIS hardware. localcoder uses it to print what a large context will cost before it spends it — prefill varies ~6x across models one fleet has approved, and the slowest is often the default on quality, so 'send the whole repo' can be three and a half minutes on one machine and thirty-five seconds on another. Measured by tools/localcoder_bench.py, declared here, never guessed: an invented rate turns a real trade into a confident wrong number.

requires.fleet_baseline: SET THIS — describe the hardware floor your team actually standardises on
requires.note: min_total_ram_gb is the fleet procurement floor, and it is compared against TOTAL physical RAM — which is what --doctor can actually measure. It was called min_free_ram_gb until 2026-08-04, and a FREE-memory floor checked against total RAM passed a 64 GB machine with 60 GB already in use. The old key is still read, and --doctor now says what it is measuring. Per-model floors live in approved_models and are what --doctor enforces for the selected model.
requires.checkers_comment: Languages this project REQUIRES a working formatter and linter for. Listing one makes --doctor FAIL on any machine where its tools are not installed, and name the install command. Use it when the project lints a language in CI and every developer therefore needs to be able to lint it locally. Empty by default: a shipped requirement would fail every adopter who has not installed that toolchain yet, and a check that is red on arrival gets ignored. Distinct from `checks.<lang>.policy`, which decides what a missing checker costs at DRAFT time; this decides what must be present at SETUP time. Known: gdscript, go, javascript, python, rust, shell, typescript.

formatters._comment: Version guards for the tools --check runs. TWO SEPARATE QUESTIONS, and a project may ask either or both. `min` is a FLOOR: 0.16 accepts 0.16.2 and 1.2.0, refuses 0.15 — it guards being too OLD (missing rules, known bugs). `expect` is a PREFIX PIN: 0.16 accepts every 0.16.x and refuses 0.17 — it guards CHURN, because --check RUNS the formatter and the formatter REWRITES the draft, so a minor bump can change the bytes committed from an identical task, and that should be a decision rather than a surprise. Empty means unguarded. Neither implies the other: a floor alone lets a major arrive silently and reformat everything; a pin alone fails a machine that is merely newer.

tasks._comment: NAMED PROMPT TEMPLATES, ONE PER KIND OF WORK. `approved_models` exists so nobody quietly runs something the team has not benchmarked; phrasing carries measurable weight too — measured on one adopting project, same model and same file, a loose brief invented every API call while one naming its context files and demanding real signatures invented none. Declare the invariants of a KIND of work here and the developer supplies only the part that is theirs: localcoder --task-template harness 'verify the trade policy'. THIS SHIPS EMPTY ON PURPOSE, like formatters.python.expect: a template states how YOUR codebase wants a kind of work done, and a guessed one is worse than none. An unknown name is a hard error, never a silent pass-through — a draft missing its invariants looks exactly like one that got them. Keys starting with _ are documentation and are never treated as templates. `localcoder --task-templates` lists what is declared; the log records which template each draft used, so the claim that phrasing moves quality is testable rather than asserted.

invariants: every check prints VERIFY OK or VERIFY FAIL with the deciding value
end with a single VERIFY RESULT line

digest._comment: EXTEND THE API-DIGEST LANGUAGE REGISTRY. tools/api_digest.py extracts the callable surface of a file — declarations plus the first doc line, never bodies — so localcoder can be given what a caller needs without the rationale comments this scaffold's own standards ask for. Measured on an adopting project: 611 lines were 41% comments and 16% declarations, ~6,900 tokens spent to convey ~900 tokens of callable surface; the digest scored the SAME on invented API calls at 33% of the tokens. On this repo, 686 KB of tools/ and ai/ reduce to 136 KB in 78 milliseconds — which is why it is generated on demand from the working tree rather than cached by a commit hook with a staleness gate. There is no staleness to gate. Python is extracted with ast; the rest by declared line patterns. Add a language here rather than editing the tool: `declaration` starts one, `body` opens an implementation block whose deeper-indented lines are skipped (without it a local variable reads as a member), `doc` is a doc comment and only the FIRST consecutive one is kept. `tools/api_digest.py --list-languages` shows what is registered.

_prefill_note: prefill_toks IS MEASURED AT REPO SCALE (~33,000 tokens), NOT AT BENCH SCALE.
It used to hold the rate tools/localcoder_bench.py reports, which is taken on ~2,000-
token drafting prompts. The field exists to answer 'what will sending the whole repo
cost me', and at that size the two numbers are not the same measurement — fixed
per-call overhead dominates a small prompt, and attention cost dominates a large one.
Measured 2026-08-09 on one M5 Max, same text, weights pre-warmed:
model                           bench ~2k    repo ~33k     33k prompt
qwen3.6:35b-a3b-coding-mxfp8        416          909           36.4s
qwen3.6:27b-coding-mxfp8            189          131          252.4s
THE ORDER IS NOT THE SAME ORDER. Ranked on the bench figure, qwen3-coder:30b leads by
4.7x and the default is fourth of five; ranked on what a repo digest actually costs,
the default is first and qwen3-coder is third. A number measured in one regime and
spent in another does not merely lose precision — here it reversed the recommendation,
and this file carried that reversed advice for a day.
The two dense 27B tags are the ones to be careful with: 3.7 and 4.2 MINUTES to read a
33k-token digest. They are the right choice for a small prompt that must be right, and
the wrong one for breadth. That is a real trade and it only appears at this size.
Re-measure when the fleet changes: a ~112,000-character prompt through /api/chat with
the model already loaded, then prompt_eval_count / prompt_eval_duration.

checks._comment: W-08: what a missing or FAILING checker means, per language. required = refuse, exit 3 (a caller running unattended must not integrate). best_effort = warn, return the draft, exit 0. off = do not check this language, and that is a decision somebody wrote down. Defaults follow the checker table: a language with a linter is required, a language with only a formatter is best_effort. LOCALCODER_CHECK_POLICY_<LANG> overrides this file.

_allow_overrides_comment: Environment variables a developer MAY use to override this project's pin. Only variables that are actually pinnable may be listed — localcoder refuses to start if this names one that is not, because a list claiming a pin that does not exist reads to a reviewer as though the question is handled (#D-09, W-20). `localcoder --where` prints the full table with the reason for each. LOCALCODER_QUIET and LOCALCODER_ROOT were removed from this list on 2026-08-11: neither can be pinned, and both had been listed since the file shipped.

_comment: YOUR OWN TOOLS, CALLED BY THE LOCAL MODEL — Splunk, Salesforce, anything speaking MCP.
The model queries them directly instead of an agent fetching data and re-typing it into
a prompt. Opt-in per call with --tools; scope with --server <name>. Guide: docs/MCP.md
PUT YOUR OWN SERVERS IN YOUR DEVICE CONFIG, NOT HERE. A server is usually a fact about
YOUR machine — your host, your token, your network — and this file is COMMITTED and
reviewed. Use ~/.config/localcoder/config.json (localcoder --init-device creates it) and
keep "extends": "device" in this file so the two combine. They merge by SERVER NAME, so
your personal servers sit alongside anything the team pins here.
THIS BLOCK IS FOR A SERVER THE WHOLE TEAM SHARES and has agreed on. Shipped empty: a
declaration is a fact about an estate, and a guessed one is worse than none, because
--tools refuses when a declared server cannot be reached.
CREDENTIALS BY REFERENCE, NEVER BY VALUE, in either file. A literal that looks like a
token is REFUSED, not warned about — by then it is already on disk.
"servers": {
"splunk_dev": {
"url": "http://splunk.example.internal:8000/en-US/splunkd/__raw/services/mcp",
"headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:SPLUNK_DEV_TOKEN}" }
MIGRATING A CLAUDE DESKTOP / CLAUDE CODE ENTRY: drop npx and mcp-remote — they exist
to turn an HTTP endpoint into a stdio one, and localcoder speaks HTTP itself. The URL
becomes "url"; --header becomes "headers". Measured: 16.7s of proxy startup against
under a second direct. The stdio form still works for a real local executable.
Then: export SPLUNK_DEV_TOKEN=... && localcoder --tools --doctor
--doctor names every server, its tool COUNT, and tells 'connected but exposes nothing'
apart from 'down' — different problems that look identical otherwise. It shows the
${env:...} reference, never the resolved token.
